## Why it exists

A database can answer `WHERE name = 'espresso machine'` in microseconds with an index. It cannot answer "espresso machines, best matches first, tolerate the typo 'espreso', show how many are under 100 dollars and how many are by each brand, and highlight the matching words", because that is not equality lookup: it is **ranking text by relevance**. `LIKE '%espresso%'` scans every row and cannot rank. Search engines exist to make this fast over millions of documents, and the technology behind them (the **inverted index**) is also the foundation of log analytics, e-commerce search, site search, code search and the keyword half of modern RAG systems.

**Mental model:** a book has a table of contents (document to words) and an **index at the back** (word to pages). A search engine builds the index at the back: for every distinct term, the list of documents containing it, with positions and counts. A query becomes a handful of term lookups and list merges, and a scoring function (**BM25** by default) ranks the documents by how well they match. Everything else (analyzers, mappings, shards, refresh) is about building that index well, keeping it fresh, and spreading it over machines.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

### The inverted index

Given three documents ("red running shoes", "blue running jacket", "red jacket"), the index looks like `red -> [1, 3]`, `running -> [1, 2]`, `shoes -> [1]`, `jacket -> [2, 3]`, `blue -> [2]`. The query `red jacket` becomes the lists for `red` and `jacket`; documents appearing in both (document 3) score higher than documents in only one. Real indexes also store term frequencies, positions (for phrase queries), and compact column-oriented **doc values** for sorting and aggregations, all compressed.

### Analysis: turning text into terms

The same **analyzer** processes text at index time and query time, so "Running", "running" and "runs" can meet. An analyzer is a **tokenizer** (split into words) plus **token filters**: lowercase, remove **stop words** ("the", "and"), apply **stemming** (running to run), expand **synonyms** (sofa to couch), fold accents. For autocomplete, **edge n-grams** index prefixes (`esp`, `espr`, `espre`...) so "esp" matches "espresso". Language matters: use the analyzer for your language, and test it with the `_analyze` API, because most "search doesn't find it" bugs are analysis mismatches.

### Relevance: BM25 in one paragraph

**BM25** scores a document for each query term using three ideas: **term frequency** (more occurrences help, with diminishing returns, so repeating a word ten times is not ten times better), **inverse document frequency** (rare terms matter more than common ones), and **field length normalization** (a match in a short title beats the same match in a long body). You then tune relevance with boosts (title counts more than description), recency or popularity functions, synonyms, and business rules. Tuning without measurement is guesswork: build a **judgment list** of queries with graded expected results and track a metric such as **nDCG** (normalized discounted cumulative gain, which rewards putting the best results first), then A/B test with real click and conversion data.

### Lucene, segments and near-real-time search

Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Solr are distributed servers built on **Apache Lucene**. Lucene writes immutable **segments**; new documents go into an in-memory buffer and become searchable at the next **refresh** (every second by default, hence "near-real-time", not instant). Deletes and updates are just marks, since segments never change; background **merges** combine segments and drop deleted documents. A **translog** (transaction log) gives durability between flushes. Consequences: very frequent refreshes cost throughput, bulk loads should relax refresh, and an update is really "delete and re-add", so frequent updates of large documents are expensive.

### Distribution: shards and replicas

An **index** is split into **primary shards**, each a complete Lucene index on some node; a query fans out to all shards and merges results. **Replica shards** are copies for availability and extra read capacity. The primary shard count is fixed when the index is created (you can split or reindex later, but plan ahead); the replica count can change any time. Guidance that has held up in practice: keep shards moderately sized (often 10 to 50 GB), avoid thousands of tiny shards (each costs memory and cluster-state overhead), and give the JVM roughly half the machine's RAM, staying below about 30 GB so compressed object pointers remain in use, leaving the rest for the operating system's page cache, which Lucene relies on heavily.

{{dg:1}}

### Mappings: the schema you cannot ignore

A **mapping** defines each field's type. The key distinction is **`text`** (analyzed, for full-text search) versus **`keyword`** (exact value, for filters, sorting, aggregations and IDs); many fields want both (`text` with a `keyword` sub-field). Other types: numbers, dates, booleans, `geo_point`, `nested` (objects whose fields must match together within one array element), and `dense_vector` for embeddings. **Dynamic mapping** guesses types from the first document it sees, which is convenient and dangerous: a field wrongly detected as `text` cannot be aggregated, and unbounded dynamic field names cause a **mapping explosion**. Define mappings explicitly in production, and treat changing a field's type as a reindex.

### Querying: query context, filter context and aggregations

- **`match`** analyzes the query text and scores matching documents; **`term`** matches an exact, unanalyzed value (use it on `keyword` fields, not `text`).
- The **`bool`** query combines clauses: `must` (required, scored), `should` (optional, boosts score), `filter` (required, not scored, cacheable) and `must_not`. Put anything that is a yes/no condition (category, price range, in stock) in **filter context**: it is faster because no score is computed, and results are cached.
- **Aggregations** compute facets and analytics (counts per brand, price histogram, average rating) in the same request.
- **Highlighting** returns snippets with matches marked; **suggesters** and "did you mean" help typos; **fuzziness** matches within an edit distance.
- **Pagination:** `from` plus `size` is limited by default to the first 10,000 hits and gets expensive deep into results. For deep or stable paging use **`search_after`** with a **point in time (PIT)**; for exporting everything, use PIT with `search_after` rather than the old scroll API.

### Beyond keywords: vectors and hybrid search

Embedding models turn text into vectors, and **approximate nearest neighbor** search (usually **HNSW**) finds semantically similar documents even without shared words. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch both support vector fields and kNN queries. **Hybrid search** runs BM25 and vector search and fuses the rankings (for example with **reciprocal rank fusion**), which usually beats either alone: keywords nail exact names, codes and rare terms; vectors catch paraphrases. Often a **reranker** (a cross-encoder model) then reorders the top results. The RAG lesson uses this stack.

### Keeping the index in sync with your database

The search index is a **derived copy**; the database stays the source of truth. Options: **dual writes** from the application (simple, but if one write fails the two diverge), the **transactional outbox** or **change data capture** (Debezium to Kafka to an indexer) for reliable, ordered updates, and periodic **full reindex** as a safety net. For schema or analyzer changes, do a **zero-downtime reindex**: build `products-v2` in the background, then atomically swap an **alias** (`products`) from v1 to v2. Applications always query the alias, never a versioned index name.

### Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and the alternatives

- **Elasticsearch** (Elastic): the original, with a strong ecosystem (Kibana, Beats and Elastic Agent) and vector and AI features. In 2021 Elastic moved from Apache 2.0 to SSPL and the Elastic License; in August 2024 it added **AGPLv3** as an option for the free parts of the code.
- **OpenSearch**: the Apache 2.0 fork of Elasticsearch 7.10, started by AWS in 2021 and now run under the Linux Foundation; Amazon OpenSearch Service is the managed offering. APIs have diverged since the fork, so client libraries and features are no longer interchangeable.
- **Versions (checked 17 October 2026, secondary sources):** Elasticsearch 9.0 shipped in April 2025 on Lucene 10, with a 9.x series continuing monthly (reports vary between 9.3 and 9.4 as the latest minor); OpenSearch 3.0 shipped in 2025 and 3.8.0 was reported on 5 August 2026.
- **Postgres full-text search** (`tsvector`, GIN indexes, `pg_trgm` for fuzzy matching) is often enough for tens of thousands to millions of documents and avoids a second system. **Typesense** and **Meilisearch** offer simple, fast, typo-tolerant search; **Algolia** and similar hosted services trade money for effort; **Solr** and **Vespa** remain strong options; **ClickHouse** and similar columnar engines serve analytics-style log queries.

When do you need a dedicated engine? When you need ranked, typo-tolerant, faceted search across large text corpora, at low latency, with relevance tuning. When you only filter and sort structured columns, a good database index is enough.

## Worked example

**1) Run a local node** (development only; security is disabled for simplicity):

```bash
docker run -d --name es -p 9200:9200 \
  -e discovery.type=single-node -e xpack.security.enabled=false \
  docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:<version>     # pin the exact tag you want
curl -s localhost:9200 | head
```

For OpenSearch, use the `opensearchproject/opensearch` image and set `OPENSEARCH_INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD`; its security plugin is on by default.

**2) Create an index with an explicit mapping and an autocomplete analyzer, bulk index, and search** (Python, `pip install elasticsearch`):

```python
from elasticsearch import Elasticsearch, helpers

es = Elasticsearch("http://localhost:9200")

es.indices.create(
    index="products-v1",
    settings={
        "number_of_shards": 1, "number_of_replicas": 0,
        "analysis": {
            "tokenizer": {"edge": {"type": "edge_ngram", "min_gram": 2, "max_gram": 15,
                                    "token_chars": ["letter", "digit"]}},
            "analyzer": {"autocomplete": {"type": "custom", "tokenizer": "edge", "filter": ["lowercase"]}},
        },
    },
    mappings={"properties": {
        "name":     {"type": "text",
                     "fields": {"keyword": {"type": "keyword"},
                                "ac": {"type": "text", "analyzer": "autocomplete", "search_analyzer": "standard"}}},
        "brand":    {"type": "keyword"},                 # exact value: filters and facets
        "price":    {"type": "float"},
        "in_stock": {"type": "boolean"},
        "created":  {"type": "date"},
    }},
)
es.indices.put_alias(index="products-v1", name="products")     # always query the alias

docs = [
    {"_index": "products", "_id": 1, "name": "Espresso machine Pro", "brand": "Brewco", "price": 129.0, "in_stock": True},
    {"_index": "products", "_id": 2, "name": "Compact espresso maker", "brand": "Brewco", "price": 79.0, "in_stock": True},
    {"_index": "products", "_id": 3, "name": "Burr coffee grinder", "brand": "Grindly", "price": 59.0, "in_stock": False},
]
helpers.bulk(es, docs, refresh="wait_for")       # make them searchable before the next call

resp = es.search(
    index="products",
    query={"bool": {
        "must":   [{"match": {"name": {"query": "espreso machine", "fuzziness": "AUTO"}}}],   # typo tolerant, scored
        "filter": [{"term": {"in_stock": True}},                                              # yes/no, not scored, cached
                   {"range": {"price": {"lte": 150}}}],
    }},
    aggs={"by_brand": {"terms": {"field": "brand"}},
          "price_ranges": {"range": {"field": "price", "ranges": [{"to": 100}, {"from": 100}]}}},
    highlight={"fields": {"name": {}}},
    size=10,
)
for hit in resp["hits"]["hits"]:
    print(round(hit["_score"], 2), hit["_source"]["name"], hit.get("highlight", {}).get("name"))
print(resp["aggregations"]["by_brand"]["buckets"])

# Autocomplete: edge n-grams on the field at index time, plain analyzer at query time
ac = es.search(index="products", query={"match": {"name.ac": "espr"}}, size=5)

# Deep paging without from/size limits: point in time + search_after
pit = es.open_point_in_time(index="products", keep_alive="1m")["id"]
page = es.search(pit={"id": pit, "keep_alive": "1m"}, size=2, sort=[{"price": "asc"}, {"_shard_doc": "asc"}],
                 query={"match_all": {}})
last_sort = page["hits"]["hits"][-1]["sort"]
page2 = es.search(pit={"id": pit, "keep_alive": "1m"}, size=2, sort=[{"price": "asc"}, {"_shard_doc": "asc"}],
                  query={"match_all": {}}, search_after=last_sort)
es.close_point_in_time(id=pit)
```

**3) A zero-downtime reindex with an alias swap** when you change the analyzer or a field type:

```python
es.indices.create(index="products-v2", settings={...}, mappings={...})     # new analyzer and mapping
es.reindex(source={"index": "products-v1"}, dest={"index": "products-v2"}, wait_for_completion=True)
es.indices.update_aliases(actions=[
    {"remove": {"index": "products-v1", "alias": "products"}},
    {"add":    {"index": "products-v2", "alias": "products"}},     # both actions apply atomically
])
# applications never noticed; delete products-v1 after a safety period
```

**4) The Postgres alternative** for modest scale, with no extra infrastructure:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, '')), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, '')), 'B')
  ) STORED;
CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search);

SELECT id, name, ts_rank_cd(search, q) AS rank
FROM products, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'espresso machine -manual') AS q
WHERE search @@ q AND in_stock
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Typo tolerance and substring search with trigrams:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX products_name_trgm ON products USING GIN (name gin_trgm_ops);
SELECT name FROM products WHERE name % 'espreso' ORDER BY similarity(name, 'espreso') DESC LIMIT 5;
```

Compare the two on your own data: Postgres full-text search is simpler to operate and transactional with your rows; a dedicated engine wins on relevance tuning, facets at scale, multilingual analysis and very large corpora.

## In real products

- **E-commerce search** (product catalogs with facets, synonyms and merchandising rules) runs on Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr, Algolia or Vespa at most large retailers; relevance tuning with judgment lists and A/B tests is a full-time discipline.
- **Log and observability platforms** store and query logs in Elasticsearch or OpenSearch (the ELK and OpenSearch Dashboards stacks), and managed observability products build on the same ideas, often with columnar stores for cost.
- **Site and documentation search** (docs sites, wikis, help centers) uses hosted engines such as Algolia, Typesense or Meilisearch for fast, typo-tolerant autocomplete.
- **GitHub code search, Wikipedia (CirrusSearch on Elasticsearch) and many internal knowledge tools** use inverted indexes tuned for their data.
- **Retrieval for AI:** RAG systems pair BM25 with vector search (hybrid retrieval and reranking) over the same documents; Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Postgres with pgvector and dedicated vector databases all appear here.
- **Security analytics (SIEM)** such as Elastic Security and Amazon OpenSearch security analytics query billions of events with the same machinery.

> [!pitfall] Using the search engine as the primary database. It is eventually consistent (refresh delay), has limited transactional guarantees, and reindexing is a normal operation. Keep the source of truth in a database and treat the index as rebuildable, with a tested reindex procedure.
> [!pitfall] Relying on dynamic mapping in production. A string field becomes `text` plus `keyword` when you wanted only `keyword`, numbers arrive as strings, and arbitrary keys create a mapping explosion that slows or crashes the cluster. Define explicit mappings and set `dynamic: strict` where the shape is known.
> [!pitfall] Analyzer mismatch and untested relevance. If index-time and query-time analysis differ unintentionally, documents silently do not match. Use `_analyze` to inspect tokens, keep a judgment list of important queries, and measure changes with nDCG or click metrics rather than eyeballing a few searches.
> [!pitfall] Too many or oversized shards, and deep pagination. Thousands of small shards exhaust heap and slow the cluster; shards in the hundreds of GB make recovery slow; `from` plus `size` deep into results is expensive and capped. Right-size shards, use rollover and lifecycle policies for time-series data, and use `search_after` with a PIT.
> [!pitfall] Putting scored `must` clauses where `filter` belongs. Yes/no conditions in query context waste CPU on scoring and miss the filter cache. Use `filter` for structured conditions and keep `must` and `should` for text relevance.
> [!security] Never expose port 9200 to the internet. Enable authentication and TLS, use role-based access with least privilege (and document or field level security where needed), prefer API keys per application, and patch promptly: exposed unauthenticated Elasticsearch and OpenSearch clusters have repeatedly led to large data leaks and ransomware. Never pass raw user input as the Query DSL; build queries from validated parameters, and think about personal data in indexed fields and logs.
> [!prod] Monitor cluster health (green, yellow, red), shard allocation, JVM heap pressure, disk watermarks, indexing and search latency, rejected requests and merge pressure. Use index templates, aliases, lifecycle management (hot, warm, cold, delete), snapshots to object storage that you have restored in a test, and rolling upgrades one version at a time as documented.
> [!cost] Search clusters are memory and disk hungry. Choose analyzers and fields deliberately (do not index fields you never search, disable `_source` bloat, avoid unneeded `text` plus `keyword` duplicates), use tiered storage and shorter retention for logs, and compare managed services, serverless options, and Postgres full-text search honestly against your real volume.
> [!tip] Start with Postgres full-text search if your corpus is small and you already run Postgres. Move to Elasticsearch or OpenSearch when relevance tuning, facets at scale, multilingual analysis or volume justify a second system, and plan from day one for how it will be fed, reindexed and monitored.
q: Why can't a LIKE '%word%' query replace a search engine?
It scans every row, cannot rank by relevance, and has no stemming, typo tolerance or facets. An inverted index maps each term to its documents so lookup and ranking are fast.
What is the difference between a text field and a keyword field?
Text fields are analyzed (tokenized, lowercased, stemmed) for full-text search. Keyword fields store the exact value, used for filters, sorting, aggregations and identifiers. Many fields need both.
Why put conditions in filter context instead of must?
Filter clauses are yes/no, are not scored and can be cached, so they are faster. Use must and should only for clauses that should affect relevance.
Why is a search index treated as a derived copy, and how do you keep it in sync?
It is eventually consistent and rebuildable, so the database stays the source of truth. Sync with a transactional outbox or change data capture, and keep a tested full reindex using an alias swap.
What does BM25 reward and penalize?
It rewards matches on rare terms and repeated terms (with diminishing returns) and penalizes long fields, so a match in a short title beats the same match in a long body.
When is Postgres full-text search enough instead of Elasticsearch?

For modest corpora and simple ranking when you already run Postgres: it is transactional with your data and needs no extra system. Move to a dedicated engine for heavy relevance tuning, facets at scale, multilingual analysis or very large volumes.
